analysis.one_liner: Gives federal health regulators authority over tobacco and bans sales and advertising aimed at minors.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a vote of any kind; it sat in a House Energy and Commerce subcommittee from June 2001 until the Congress ended in January 2003.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have given the Secretary of Health and Human Services, acting through the FDA, the power to regulate tobacco products for the first time. It banned selling tobacco to anyone under 18, restricted how tobacco could be sold, banned advertising aimed at young people, required makers to disclose their ingredients and nicotine content, and let the FDA set product standards and recall defective products. It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and then to its Health subcommittee, where it died without a hearing, a vote, or any further action.
analysis.who_benefits: Young people, who would face far fewer legal channels to start smoking; families and communities that bear the costs of tobacco-related disease; and the public generally, through ingredient disclosure and FDA oversight of a product that causes cancer, heart disease, and addiction.

how_it_helps.text: The bill amends the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act to give the Secretary of Health and Human Services regulatory authority over tobacco products, a power the Supreme Court had held the FDA did not have on its own.

It prohibits selling tobacco to anyone under 18, limits sales to face-to-face transactions (with narrow exceptions for mail order and adults-only vending machines), and makes it illegal to target youth in tobacco advertising.

Manufacturers must disclose all ingredients and nicotine content to the government, register their facilities, and submit research on health effects; the public gets access to registration information.
The bill's own findings estimate that cutting youth smoking in half would prevent well over 60,000 early deaths each year and save up to $43 billion annually in medical costs and lost productivity.

The FDA could set performance standards (such as reducing nicotine or harmful constituents), require premarket review of new tobacco products, and order recalls of products with manufacturing defects that cause serious health harm.

analysis.who_pays: Tobacco manufacturers, importers, and their advertisers bear the cost of registration, ingredient disclosure, premarket review, and marketing restrictions. Retailers lose self-service and vending-machine sales to minors. Some compliance costs would likely be passed to adult consumers through higher prices, and adult buyers would face narrower purchasing channels.

drawbacks.text: The bill preempts state and local rules that are stricter than the federal ones on labeling, performance standards, and manufacturing, which could override tougher state tobacco laws in those areas, though states keep authority over sales and access rules.

It restricts how adults can buy tobacco: retail sales must be face-to-face except for limited mail-order sales and vending machines in adults-only facilities, which adds inconvenience and compliance costs for legitimate adult customers and small retailers.

The bill entirely exempts tobacco growers and farms from FDA authority — FDA employees cannot even enter a tobacco farm without written consent — leaving the raw-leaf end of the supply chain unregulated.

Registration, disclosure, and good-manufacturing requirements impose real costs on manufacturers and retailers, which an honest supporter would acknowledge are likely to be passed on to consumers in higher prices.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit — cutting off the pipeline that gets children addicted to a product the bill itself calls a cause of cancer and heart disease — is large and well-documented in the bill's findings. The costs are real but modest by comparison: inconvenience for adult purchasers, compliance costs for sellers, and a preemption provision that could override some stricter state rules. The bill is not badly designed, though its total carve-out for tobacco growers shows where its ambition stopped.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and then to its Health subcommittee, where it sat for the rest of the Congress without a hearing or vote and expired in January 2003.

narrative.text: Rep. Tom Davis (R-VA) introduced the bill on June 14, 2001, with 14 original cosponsors joining him at introduction.
The House referred it to the Committee on Energy and Commerce the day it was introduced.
On June 25, 2001, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Health, the last committee action the bill ever received.
The sponsor delivered additional introductory remarks in March 2002, but no hearing, markup, or vote followed.
The bill attracted 19 cosponsors in total — 12 Republicans and 7 Democrats — and never reached the House floor before the 107th Congress ended on January 3, 2003.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Tobacco manufacturers, distributors, and retailers are better off, because no federal regulator gained authority over their products, marketing, or ingredient disclosure. Young people gained nothing, since the protections for them never took effect.

for.name: Rep. Tom Davis
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on it twice, in June 2001 and March 2002.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee and its Health Subcommittee
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on June 14, 2001 and the subcommittee referral on June 25, 2001, and never reported the bill, held a hearing, or scheduled a vote.

against.name: Tobacco industry
against.role: Manufacturers, distributors, and advertisers of tobacco products
against.what_they_did: Opposed federal regulation of tobacco products, which would have subjected their manufacturing, ingredients, and marketing to FDA oversight for the first time.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's support was bipartisan from the start — 12 Republicans and 7 Democrats signed on — but with only 19 cosponsors in a 435-member House, it never generated the momentum needed to move through committee.

industries.note: The bill would have subjected them to FDA registration, annual ingredient and nicotine disclosure, premarket review of new products, performance standards, and recall authority. Its own findings attribute youth addiction substantially to industry marketing.

Sales to anyone under 18 would be prohibited, and sales would be restricted to face-to-face transactions with narrow exceptions, eliminating vending-machine and mail-order channels that now reach young customers.

Youth-targeted advertising would be banned outright, and any advertising that violates the Act would become an unfair or deceptive practice enforceable under the Federal Trade Commission Act — a direct hit to the promotional spending the bill's findings say drives adolescent smoking.

The bill carves them out entirely: FDA has no authority over tobacco leaf production and cannot even enter a tobacco farm without the grower's written consent. Growers lose nothing under the bill, in a clear accommodation the manufacturers' side of the industry did not receive.
